hook.text: A data model is only a drawing until code loads it, and that code is usually Python. Say the input is a fifty gigabyte log, and the machine has eight gigabytes of memory.

hook-fit.text: [slowly] Read the whole file first, and it can't fit. Read it one line at a time, and memory only ever holds a line.

plan.text: That's what the Python round checks: code that moves data without running out of memory, and is safe to run twice. Eighteen questions: fourteen worked through, each run in Python, then four quickly.

gen-in.text: It starts with one choice: a list, or a generator.

gen.text: Question one. Why prefer a generator over a list when processing large data?

gen-yield.text: A list holds every element at once. A generator yields one at a time, on demand. The page's parser reads a line, splits it, and yields a name and a quantity.

gen-million.text: On a file of a million orders, collecting the rows in a list peaks at sixty-three megabytes. Summing straight from the generator peaks at about a hundred fifty kilobytes.

gen-flat.text: Cut the file to a tenth, and so does the list. The generator doesn't move: its memory doesn't depend on the input.

pipe.text: Question two. How do generator pipelines compare to building intermediate lists?

pipe-swap.text: Here's a three-stage pipeline, twice. With square brackets, each stage is a list, and all three are alive at once: a hundred sixty megabytes. With round brackets, each is a generator, and one row passes through all three before the next is read.

pipe-trade.text: Lists still earn their place: you can print one to debug it, and read it twice. A generator is spent after one pass; sum it again, and you get zero. Lists for small data you rescan, generators for large or endless data.

file-in.text: Which is how you read a file.

file.text: Question three. How do you process a file too big to fit in memory?

file-read.text: Don't call read or read lines. On the same eight megabyte file, read holds the whole text: seventeen megabytes. Read lines holds every line: thirty-four.

file-loop.text: A file object is already a lazy iterator over its lines, so a plain for loop streams it, in about a hundred fifty kilobytes. Chain generators on it, and nothing is read until the last one asks.

csv.text: Question four. How do you process a large CSV with pandas without loading it all?

csv-chunks.text: Pass chunk size to read CSV, and you get an iterator of data frames: ten chunks of a hundred thousand rows. Sum each chunk by group, and fold it into a counter.

csv-same.text: The totals match the whole-file read exactly, and memory peaks at one chunk: seven and a half megabytes, not fifty-four.

csv-mean.text: Sums add up across chunks. A mean doesn't: the mean of the chunks' means is off. Carry the sum and the count, and divide at the end.

iter-in.text: That one pass deserves a closer look.

iter.text: Question five. What's the difference between an iterable and an iterator?

iter-def.text: [slowly] An iterable, like a list or a dict, hands out a fresh iterator each time you loop over it. An iterator keeps its place, and once it reaches the end, it's used up.

iter-twice.text: Read the list twice: four rows, then four again. Read the generator twice: four, then zero. A generator is an iterator, and so is an open file.

iter-trap.text: Here's how it bites: count the rows for the log, then load them. Four counted, zero loaded, and no error. For two passes, make a list, or create the generator again.

hash-in.text: Next, how a set answers without looking.

hash.text: Question six. Why are dict and set lookups order one, and when does that matter?

hash-scan.text: A list doesn't know where a value lives, so a membership test compares from the front: a million comparisons for the last of a million numbers.

hash-jump.text: Dicts and sets are hash tables. Hashing the value picks one bucket out of two million, and Python goes straight there: one comparison, at any size.

hash-time.text: Timed in CPython, that's five and a half milliseconds, against twenty-three nanoseconds.

hash-loop.text: It matters inside a loop. Deduplicate ten thousand records against a list of the ones you've seen: fifty million comparisons. Double the records, and it's four times as many, order n squared. A set makes it one lookup a record.

dedup.text: Question seven. How do you deduplicate records in memory?

dedup-set.text: One pass, with a set of the keys you've seen. User one's second record is skipped, and each user's first is kept, in order: one, two, three.

dedup-dict.text: To keep the latest instead, map each key to a record in a dict, and replace it when a later timestamp arrives.

latest.text: Question eight. How do you keep only the latest record per key in pandas?

latest-sort.text: Sort by timestamp, drop duplicates on the key, and keep the last. ID one keeps b, from time twenty: the pandas version of row number equals one in sequel.

latest-tie.text: [slowly] If two rows can share a timestamp, add a tiebreaker to the sort, so which one you keep doesn't depend on arrival order.

join-in.text: A dict can do a join, too.

join.text: Question nine. How do you join two datasets in memory without a database?

join-build.text: Build a dict from the smaller side, keyed on the join column: user ID to name. Then scan the larger side, and look up each order's user.

join-cost.text: That's a hash join, order n plus m. Comparing every order with every user is order n times m.

join-miss.text: The follow-up: an order whose user isn't there. Square brackets raise a key error. Get returns none and keeps the order, as a left join would.

batch-in.text: Writing it out has its own pattern.

batch.text: Question ten. How do you split a large stream into fixed-size batches?

batch-why.text: An insert per row pays a round trip per row. A million rows in batches of a thousand is a thousand calls.

batch-slice.text: Pull n items at a time from the iterator with i-slice, until a pull comes back empty. Seven items in threes: three, three, and a last batch of one.

batch-builtin.text: Since Python three twelve, itertools batched does exactly this.

retry-in.text: And when a call fails, you retry it, carefully.

retry.text: Question eleven. How do you make a network call resilient with retries and backoff?

retry-loop.text: Catch transient errors, wait, and try again, doubling the wait each time. Here the call fails twice, waits ten milliseconds, then twenty, and succeeds on the third try.

retry-herd.text: Then add jitter. Model six clients failing in one outage: with plain backoff, they all come back together, at one, three, seven and fifteen seconds.

retry-jitter.text: Wait a random time up to each delay instead, and their retries spread out.

retry-not.text: Know what not to retry, too. A bad request fails the same way every time, so it's raised at once. Cap the attempts, and retry only what's safe to repeat: a retried payment can charge twice.

idem-in.text: Safe to repeat has a name.

idem.text: Question twelve. What makes a transform idempotent, and how do you write one in Python?

idem-def.text: It ends in the same state however many times it runs, which makes retries and backfills safe.

idem-append.text: Append a batch, rerun it after a failure, and four rows record two events.

idem-upsert.text: Write by key instead. The page's upsert sets each ID's status, and the second run changes nothing.

idem-add.text: Keyed isn't enough on its own. Add each payment into its key, run it twice, and every total doubles. Set values; don't add to them.

clean.text: Question thirteen. How do you clean messy delimited records defensively?

clean-page.text: Strip whitespace, check the field count, and convert types without letting one row crash the job. Bob's missing age becomes none; bad row is dropped.

clean-csv.text: Split on commas yourself, and a quoted name, Smith comma Jo, becomes four fields. The CSV module reads three.

clean-reject.text: [slowly] And don't drop bad rows in silence. Send them to a reject list with the reason, and count them.

parse.text: Question fourteen. How do you parse numbers or dates that might be malformed?

parse-num.text: In pandas, to numeric with errors equals coerce turns what won't parse into not a number: n slash a, and twelve hundred with a comma. Count them, so they don't vanish into an average.

parse-date.text: For dates, parse with an explicit format, and catch the value error. A day-first date fails, and so does February thirtieth.

r-stream.text: To aggregate a stream without holding rows, fold each record into a running dict as it arrives. Memory grows with the groups, not the rows: here, two.

r-pandas.text: Reach for pandas when the data fits in memory and you want vectorized columns, group by and joins. Stay with generators when it streams, or won't fit.

r-groupby.text: Group by splits the rows by key, sums each group, and combines the answers. As index equals false keeps the region as a column: EU two twenty-five, US one fifty.

r-pitfalls.text: And the common pitfalls: membership tests against a list, strings built with plus in a loop, iter rows where a column operation exists, a data frame grown concat by concat, and a whole file read that could stream.

next.text: Put these together, run them every night on a schedule, and one script has become a pipeline. Next: pipelines and systems.
